name: Prompt Templates and Regression Tests
question: How do I change a prompt without breaking it?
summary: Treat prompts as code. Build them from templates with named variables and shared blocks, fail loudly when a variable is missing, wrap untrusted variables in tags, and keep stable text before variable text. Every change runs a regression suite of golden cases in CI before it can ship, and versions are released through a registry, as Panel 11 describes.
useCases: Prompts edited by several people or changed weekly
Many prompts sharing the same rules or policy text
Any prompt whose failures are costly

items.detail: Jinja2 or similar, with includes for shared blocks
StrictUndefined: a missing variable raises instead of rendering blank
untrusted variables are wrapped in tags and escaped
stable text first for caching; variables and the question last
real inputs with expected outputs or graded criteria
a change cannot merge unless the suite passes

steps.title: Prompts live in template files
steps.text: Shared rules sit in one reviewed include used by every prompt, instead of being copied and drifting apart.

steps.title: Missing variables fail loudly
steps.text: With StrictUndefined, forgetting the ticket raises an error in tests rather than sending a prompt with a blank where the customer’s text should be.

steps.title: Wrap and escape untrusted text
steps.text: The ticket goes inside tags and is escaped, so it reads as data and cannot close the tag early.

steps.title: Stable text first
steps.text: The shared rules come first and never change between calls, which keeps the prefix cacheable; the ticket comes last.

steps.title: Test against a golden set
steps.text: 300 real tickets with grading criteria. A change that breaks an intent seen in 3% of traffic is almost certainly covered.

steps.title: Gate the merge in CI
steps.text: Any change under prompts/ runs the suite. A failing case blocks the merge, before a version is ever promoted.

practice.scenario: A SaaS company’s support prompts were f-strings edited by three teams. A missing variable once rendered as “None” in thousands of replies, and a policy edit silently broke refunds for annual plans, a 3% intent. Prompts now live in Jinja2 templates with strict variables and shared includes, and a 300-case golden suite runs in CI on every change.

Regulated wording kept in one reviewed include used by every prompt
Seasonal prompt changes tested against last season’s tricky cases

practice.analogy: A legal contract built from approved clause templates. Nobody retypes a clause, and every new version is checked against the old cases before signing.

numericDrill.question: A prompt change breaks an intent that makes up 3% of traffic. Your golden suite has 100 cases sampled from traffic. What is the chance that at least one case covers that intent, in percent?
numericDrill.answer: 1 − 0.97¹⁰⁰ ≈ 1 − 0.048 = 95.2%. With 20 cases it is only 45.6%; with 300 it is over 99.9%. Rare intents need bigger suites or deliberate coverage.

interview.question: Why use StrictUndefined in Jinja2 prompt templates?
interview.answer: By default a missing variable renders as an empty string, so a prompt can silently lose the customer’s data or a policy block. StrictUndefined raises an error at render time, which tests and CI catch before release.

interview.question: How do you build a good golden set for prompt regression tests?
interview.answer: Sample real inputs from production across intents, deliberately add rare but important cases and past failures, and write assertions or rubrics for each. Keep it versioned, grow it whenever an incident reveals a gap, and run it in CI on every prompt change.
